For two terms he was director general of the Punjab police force, and was credited with having brought the [[Punjab insurgency]] under control. There are accusations that he and the forces under his command were responsible for "multiple cases of human rights violation", "in the name of" stamping out terrorism.{{cite web|publisher=Amnesty International|title=A mockery of justice: The case concerning the "disappearance" of human rights defender Jaswant Singh Khalra severely undermined|url=http://web.amnesty.org/library/Index/ENGASA200071998?open&of=ENG-IND|date=20 July 1999|access-date=29 November 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071017113415/http://web.amnesty.org/library/Index/ENGASA200071998?open&of=ENG-IND|archive-date=17 October 2007}}{{cite news| last = Singh| first = Jangveer| title = K.P.S. Gill visited Khalra in jail, says witness : Recounts tale of police brutality before his 'murder'| work = The Tribune| date = 17 February 2005| url = http://www.tribuneindia.com/2005/20050217/punjab1.htm| access-date = 29 November 2008| archive-date = 5 October 2008| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081005034823/http://www.tribuneindia.com/2005/20050217/punjab1.htm| url-status = live}} He was also convicted in a sexual harassment case.{{cite news |title=Watch: Rupan Deol Bajaj talks about the sexual harassment case she won against KPS Gill |url=https://scroll.in/video/839715/watch-rupan-deol-bajaj-talks-about-the-sexual-harassment-case-she-won-against-kps-gill |work=Scroll |date=5 June 2017 |access-date=19 March 2022 |archive-date=9 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220209075415/https://scroll.in/video/839715/watch-rupan-deol-bajaj-talks-about-the-sexual-harassment-case-she-won-against-kps-gill |url-status=live }} Gill retired from the IPS in 1995. Gill was also an author and editor, and was president of the [[Indian Hockey Federation]] for fifteen years, until he resigned following a corruption scandal. ==Early life== Gill was born on 29 6 April 2006| access-date = 13 March 2008}} from 1988 to 1990 and then again from 1991 until his retirement from the Indian Police Service in 1995. During this era when [[Sikh extremism|Sikh extremists]] in the [[Khalistan movement]] were active in Punjab, there were reports of [[Human rights in Punjab, India|human rights violations in the Punjab region]]. [[Amnesty International]] reported that, from 1983 to 1994, armed groups "struggling" to form an [[Khalistan|independent Sikh state]], assassinating perpetrators of the [[1984 anti-Sikh riots|1984 Sikh pogroms]] or [[Indian National Congress|Congress Party]] members, and taking hostages. It further reported that the police responded with a crackdown, "illegally detaining, torturing and killing hundreds of young men".{{cite web|url=http://www.amnestyusa.org/document.php?lang=e&id=F072BE8A8A0506C08025690000692C86|title=India: A vital opportunity to end impunity in Punjab|date=1998–1999|publisher=[[Amnesty International]]|access-date=4 July 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090625031306/http://www.amnestyusa.org/document.php?id=F072BE8A8A0506C08025690000692C86&lang=e|archive-date=25 June 2009}} [[Human Rights Watch]] (HRW) reported that from the 1980s Sikh separatists were guilty of targeted assassinations and attacks upon [[Punjabi Hindus|Hindu minorities in the Punjab state]]. HRW also reported that the government response resulted in further serious "human rights violations against tens of thousands".{{cite web|url=https://www.hrw.org/en/news/2007/10/17/india-time-deliver-justice-atrocities-punjab|title=India: Time to Deliver Justice for Atrocities in Punjab: Investigate and Prosecute Perpetrators of 'Disappearances' and Killings|date=17 October 2007|publisher=[[Human Rights Watch]]|access-date=4 July 2009|archive-date=10 June 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090610000359/http://www.hrw.org/en/news/2007/10/17/india-time-deliver-justice-atrocities-punjab|url-status=live}}{{cite news|url=http://www.tribuneindia.com/2004/20040730/nhrc1.htm|title=The following is the text of the public notice issued by the National Human Rights Commission in The Tribune, on July 15, 2004.|date=15 July 2004|work=REFERENCE CASE NO. 1/97/NHRC (Arising out of the order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India dated December 12, 1996 and September 10, 1998 in Writ Petition No. 447/95 and 497/95)|access-date=5 July 2009|archive-date=13 August 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090813204106/http://www.tribuneindia.com/2004/20040730/nhrc1.htm|url-status=live}} HRW report in 1991 described the security forces using "increasingly brutal methods to stem the militant movement, resulting in widespread human rights violations." Thousands of civilians and suspected militants were summarily executed in "staged" [[encounter killing]]s. Many "disappeared" while in police custody and thousands were detained without trial and subjected to torture. The post-1991 period coincides with Gill's second tenure as Director General of Punjab police. It is this period that witnessed the most serious escalation of violence. In May 1988, he commanded [[Operation Black Thunder#Operation Black Thunder II|Operation Black Thunder]] to flush out militants hiding in the [[Harmandir Sahib|Golden Temple]]. Compared to [[Operation Blue Star]], little damage was inflicted on the Golden Temple.{{Cite news |last=Hazarika |first=Sanjoy |last2=Times |first2=Special To the New York |date=18 May 1988 |title=INDIAN COMMANDOS CLOSE IN ON SIKHS |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/05/18/world/indian-commandos-close-in-on-sikhs.html |access-date=5 July 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} In what was reported as a successful operation, around 67 [[Sikhs]] surrendered and 4 were killed in the encounter. Gill stated that he did not want to repeat the mistakes made by Indian army during Operation Blue Star.{{Cite news |last=Hazarika |first=Sanjoy |last2=Times |first2=Special To the New York |date=19 May 1988 |title=Sikhs Surrender to Troops at Temple |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/05/19/world/sikhs-surrender-to-troops-at-temple.html |access-date=5 July 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} In contrast to prior operations, minimum force was used under full public scrutiny.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=z9GG4__JJNwC&pg=PA398 |title=Terrorism in context By Martha Crenshaw |access-date=28 September 2009 | isbn=978-0-271-01015-1|year=1995|last1=Crenshaw |first1=Martha |publisher=Penn State Press }}{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20110606084435/http://www.hindustantimes.com/StoryPage/StoryPage.aspx?id=fba3dc2a-db08-405e-8506-f220d7690d47|title=Black Thunder’s silver lining}}, ''[[Hindustan Times]]'', 13 May 2008 1991 saw the peak of violence in Punjab, with more than 5000 reported killed. In 1992, the Indian government, intent on retaking Punjab from terrorism, appointed Gill as Chief of Police in Punjab. The police and army instituted a crackdown, and in 1993 the reported death toll was less than 500. In 1993, ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported, the people of Punjab no longer feared the Sikh rebels or gangs, but instead feared the army and police.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/10/26/world/though-sikh-rebellion-is-quelled-india-s-punjab-state-still-seethes.html?pagewanted=1|title=Though Sikh Rebellion Is Quelled, India's Punjab State Still Seethes|last=Gargan|first=Edward A.|date=26 October 1993|work=The New York Times|access-date=5 July 2009}} Patricia Gossman describes Gill as having a goal to eliminate, not merely arrest, militant Sikh leaders and members. KPS Gill also expanded a bounty system of rewards for police who killed known militants – a practice that encouraged the police to resort to [[Extrajudicial killing|extrajudicial executions]] and disappearances.{{cite book|last=Gossman|first=Patricia|title=Death Squads in Global Perspective|year=2002|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|pages=264, 269}} The police were awarded financially for killing militants. [[Government of India|India's central government]] created a special fund to finance Punjab's death squads, to pay the network of informants who provided information about militants and those suspected of supporting militants, and to reward police who captured and killed them.{{cite book|last=Gossman|first=Patricia|title=Death Squads in Global Perspective|year=2002|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|pages=269}} The reward was about [[Indian rupee sign|₹]]50,000 ([[Dollar sign|$]]1,670). In an article in ''[[India Today]]'' on 15 October 1992 it was written that the rush of claiming cash rewards is turning police into mercenaries. Besides the rewards for killing militants (annual outlay for the purpose: {{INR}}1.13 [[crore]] [$338,000]), the department gives 'unannounced rewards' for killing unlisted militants.{{cite news|last=Sandhu|first=Kanwar|title=Official Excesses|newspaper=India Today|date=15 October 1992}} Gill retired from the IPS in 1995. He was going to be employed as the Governor of Punjab, but could not due to criminal cases he was facing, and after Beant Singh was assassinated he was immediately sent off. ===1995–1999=== Gill founded the Institute for Conflict Management (ICM){{cite web |url=http://www.rediff.com/news/1999/jun/12inter.htm |title=The Rediff Interview/ K P S Gill: 'Few months is too short a period to say Bus Diplomacy has failed ' |work=Rediff.com |date=12 June 1999 |access-date=28 September 2009 |archive-date=3 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303183709/http://www.rediff.com/news/1999/jun/12inter.htm |url-status=live }} and was its first president.{{cite web|url=http://in.rediff.com/news/2008/apr/20gill.htm |title=Muslims are the victims of global jihad: K P S Gill |work=Rediff.com |date=20 April 2008 |access-date=28 September 2009}} Gill began advising governments on counter-terrorism matters. In 1997, the Chief minister of [[Assam]] state, [[Prafulla Kumar Mahanta]], requested his services as security advisor. However, since the sexual harassment case against him was pending he was not able to take this appointment.[http://www.indianexpress.com/ie/daily/20000521/profile.htm Supercop to the rescue]{{dead link|date=November 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, ''[[The Indian Express]]'', 21 May 2000 In 1999, [[Delhi Police]] arrested Richhpal Singh, who was allegedly a [[Babbar Khalsa]] [[suicide attack|suicide bomber]] on a mission to assassinate Gill. He arrived in [[Delhi]] from [[Pakistan]] on an [[Afghanistan|Afghan]] passport. Two kilograms of the explosive [[RDX]], four [[detonator]]s, and some 'live wire'{{clarify|date=July 2009}} were recovered from him.[http://www.rediff.com/news/1999/jun/07bomb.htm Suicide bomber nabbed in Delhi] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303200751/http://www.rediff.com/news/1999/jun/07bomb.htm |date=3 March 2016 }}, [[Rediff.com]], 7 June 1999 In an interview after this incident, Gill claimed that he had been a target of four or five such assassination attempts by Babbar Khalsa and other Sikh militant groups. Gill stated that he was not afraid.[http://www.rediff.com/news/1999/jun/12inter.htm 'Few months is too short a period to say Bus Diplomacy has failed '] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303183709/http://www.rediff.com/news/1999/jun/12inter.htm |date=3 March 2016 }}, [[Rediff.com]], 12 June 1999 ===2000–2004=== In 2000 the government of [[Sri Lanka]] sought his expertise as an anti-terrorism expert to help them draw a comprehensive counter-terrorism strategy against [[Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam]][http://www.expressindia.com/news/ie/daily/20000517/ina17039.html KPS Gill to advise Lanka on security] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120928184329/http://www.expressindia.com/news/ie/daily/20000517/ina17039.html |date=28 September 2012 }}, ''[[The Indian Express]]'', 16 May 2000 He was approached by [[Lakshman Kadirgamar]] who was the foreign minister of Sri Lanka[http://www.hindu.com/2000/05/18/stories/0218000q.htm K.P.S. Gill gearing for assignment in Sri Lanka] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121105022601/http://www.hindu.com/2000/05/18/stories/0218000q.htm |date=5 November 2012 }}, [[The Hindu]], 17 May 2000 After the defeat of [[Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam]] the similarity in the tactics used by Sri Lanka with the tactics used by Gill in Punjab was noted in an article published in [[India Today]]{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120715161133/http://indiatoday.intoday.in/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=43637§ionid=64&secid=0&Itemid=1&issueid=71|title='Sri Lanka won by throwing away the rulebook'}}, [[India Today]], 24 May 2009 Gill was appointed as security adviser to the state of [[Gujarat]] after [[2002 Gujarat violence]]. Gujarat Chief minister [[Narendra Modi]], commenting on his appointment, stated, "It is good to have an experienced person such as Gill as my security advisor. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill (29 December 1934 – 26 May 2017) was an Indian Police Service (IPS) officer. For two terms he was director general of the Punjab police force, and was credited with having brought the Punjab insurgency under control. There are accusations that he and the forces under his command were responsible for "multiple cases of human rights violation", "in the name of" stamping out terrorism. He was also convicted in a sexual harassment case. Gill retired from the IPS in 1995.
Gill was also an author and editor, and was president of the Indian Hockey Federation for fifteen years, until he resigned following a corruption scandal.
